title: The Dog-Headed Question: Ansgar's Fosterling, the Danish Field, and the Book That Was Lost for Six Hundred Years
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Torhout, a birth the sources cannot agree on
stops.date_confidence: traditional; year conventional, birthplace disputed. German Wikipedia and the Oekumenisches Heiligenlexikon give Flemish nobility near Torhout; English Wikipedia states that historians widely accept a Danish origin. Neither position is adjudicated here, and the pin sits at Torhout only because it is the one named place either tradition offers.
stops.campa: A boy is born in the years when the Frankish empire begins coming apart, and the record cannot say where. One tradition puts him among the nobility of Flanders, on or near the manor of Turholt that the northern mission holds in these decades. Another puts his ancestors among the Danes, which would make the future archbishop of the Danish mission a Dane. Both traditions are old, both are still defended, and neither can be dismissed. What comes down is a name and a childhood spent within reach of a church already looking north. Was the child a Fleming or a Dane?
suggested_refs: The Vita Rimberti, anonymous, written at Corvey c. 900, the only life of him and the source of the Flemish tradition

stops.name: Torhout, the manor given to the northern mission
stops.date_confidence: attested for the grant, c. 831; Rimbert's presence on the estate in these particular years is inference from his later training there
stops.campa: Louis the Pious gives the manor of Turholt to Ansgar so that a mission to the pagan north can be paid for out of Flemish grain. The arrangement is exact: crops from a rich estate in the west feed preachers who sail from the mouth of the Elbe. In the 840s Charles the Bald takes the manor back for his own men, and the mission loses its endowment in the same decade the Danish fleets burn Hamburg. Money and cathedral go within a few years of each other. Rimbert learns his letters in the house that had been paying for the north.
suggested_refs: The Turholt endowment, granted by Louis the Pious and withdrawn by Charles the Bald, the financial spine of the Scandinavian mission
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, tr. Charles H. Robinson (1921)

stops.name: Torhout, the psalter before anything else
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the Vita Rimberti is hagiography written c. 900 by a monk of Corvey, and the Heiligenlexikon warns in as many words that it contains much that is legendary
stops.campa: The boy is raised inside a religious household on the estate and set to the psalter before he is set to anything else. His biographer, a monk of Corvey writing some seventy years after his death, insists the marks of holiness were on him from infancy, that he would not play at what other children played and went to prayer instead. The same biographer reports miracles no other source knows. Under the hagiography there is a psalter, the one book the mission owns in every house it keeps, and a child on an estate in Flanders being taught to read out of it.
suggested_refs: The collegiate church on the Turholt estate, where the training of the mission's clergy was done

stops.name: Bremen, entering the household of Ansgar
stops.date_confidence: inferred; no source dates his entry into Ansgar's household, and c. 850 is read backward from the shape of the career
stops.campa: Rimbert comes into the household of Ansgar at Bremen and does not leave it again for fifteen years. The Vita Rimberti calls him the archbishop's alumnus, his fosterling in the faith. He is secretary, companion on the road, and in the end the man at the bedside. He hears the north described first as talk in this house, by the only person alive who has seen the Swedish mission from inside it, who has been robbed at sea on the way there, and who has watched Hamburg burn.
suggested_refs: The archiepiscopal household at Bremen, seat of the mission after the sack of Hamburg in 845

stops.name: Nordalbingia, the circuit north of the Elbe
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the general shape of Hamburg-Bremen's mission territory; no source names a village or a year
stops.campa: He rides the pastoral circuit with Ansgar through the marsh parishes north of the Elbe, the raw edge of Saxon Christianity, where the Danish raiders and the Danish converts are sometimes the same families. No document names the places or the seasons. He learns on horseback what a diocese is out here: a line of small wooden churches held by consent, and the consent renewed every year. One bad summer at sea can undo a decade of it. He rides the circuit for years before he is asked to run it.
suggested_refs: The Nordalbingian marsh parishes, the Elbe frontier of Carolingian Saxony
sources: general context of the Hamburg-Bremen mission territory

stops.name: Schleswig, a priest named Rimbert is sent to the Danes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the ordination and the mission, undated in the source; the identification of this priest with the author of the Vita is doubted by Robinson's own footnote and is the oldest open question in the biography
stops.campa: Ansgar ordains a priest for the Danish work and sends him over the frontier, where the king and the people receive him and he celebrates the mysteries without hindrance. The Vita Anskarii names that priest Rimbert and says his ancestors were Danes. If that is the same Rimbert who wrote the sentence, the Danish-origin tradition has a source close to the bone. Robinson's footnote objects that by Adam of Bremen's reckoning Rimbert could only have been a deacon in these years, and a deacon is not the priest in the sentence. Is the writer the priest? The footnote raises it and stops there.
stops.quote: he ordained for this work a priest named Rimbert, whose ancestors were of Danish extraction. When he had sent him in Christ's name to those parts he was kindly received there by the king and the people, and by the help of the Lord he celebrated without restraint the divine mysteries in their midst.
stops.quote_source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. XXXIII, tr. Charles H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (1921), p. 104. Robinson's footnote: It is not clear whether this Rimbert is to be identified with the author of the Life of Anskar.
suggested_refs: Robinson's footnote at Vita Anskarii ch. XXXIII, raising and leaving open the identification
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. XXXIII, tr. Robinson (1921), p. 104
Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis, via Robinson's apparatus, not read directly

stops.name: Bremen, the prayer book drawn out of the old man
stops.date_confidence: attested as an episode, undated; Robinson's footnote identifies the unnamed friend as probably Rimbert, which is inference and not statement
stops.campa: Ansgar keeps a private book of prayers, verses gathered out of the psalms and arranged for his own use, which he sings to himself and shows to nobody. One of his people works on him at length until the old man consents to dictate it out. The friend then keeps the copy secret for as long as Ansgar lives and lets it be read only after the funeral. If that friend is Rimbert, the first thing he ever took down from his master is a text his master did not want circulated. Robinson's note says probably. The note is an editor's inference and not the book's statement.
stops.quote: One of us who was a special friend of his persuaded with difficulty and after much entreaty to dictate to him exactly that which he was wont to sing, but as long as he lived he made known to no one what he had written, though after Anskar's death he showed it to those who desired to read it.
stops.quote_source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. XXXV, tr. Charles H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (1921), p. 111
suggested_refs: Ansgar's pigmenta, the private collection of psalm-verses dictated under pressure and withheld until his death
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. XXXV, tr. Robinson (1921), p. 111

stops.name: The frontier beyond the Danes, a report of men who bark
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Ratramnus's reply refers to a report that had reached Rimbert but fixes neither a place nor a date, and the pin here stands for an unmapped remainder rather than a location
stops.campa: Somewhere past the last church the mission can supply, at the edge of what Bremen's priests can reach and return from, a report is picked up: a people who do not speak but bark, dog-headed, living in villages of their own. Whoever carried the report is not named. Where they had been is not written down. The report is not handled as a marvel to be retold at table. It is handled as a jurisdictional problem, because if there are men out there, they are owed preaching, and the man responsible for preaching to them would be the archbishop of the north.
suggested_refs: Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de Cynocephalis, which preserves the report only by answering it
sources: Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de Cynocephalis, via English Wikipedia, 'Ratramnus'; the Latin at Patrologia Latina 121:1153-56 was not retrieved

stops.name: Bremen, the letter south to Corbie
stops.date_confidence: before 865; the MGH title of the reply addresses Rimbert as presbyter and not as archbishop, and Ratramnus died c. 868, giving a window of the late 850s to 865. This contradicts Robinson's note that Rimbert was still a deacon in 865, and neither can be checked against the other here.
stops.campa: Rimbert, still a priest and nobody's successor yet, writes to a monk of Corbie he has never met and asks the question a missionary cannot leave alone: do the cynocephali possess rational souls, and may they be baptized. He is not asking whether the story is true. He is asking what he is obliged to do if it is. The letter itself does not survive. Everything known about it comes from the answer, which restates the question before taking it up, and which addresses him as presbyter, a rank he holds only before 865.
suggested_refs: MGH, Epistolae Karolini aevi, Epist. de cynocephalis ad Rimbertum presbyterum scripta, whose title dates the exchange
sources: Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de Cynocephalis, manuscript tradition

stops.name: Corbie, Ratramnus answers
stops.date_confidence: attested that Ratramnus of Corbie answered with the Epistola de Cynocephalis; the year is a placement inside the pre-865 window, not an attestation
stops.campa: Ratramnus of Corbie takes the question seriously enough to answer it with argument instead of wonder. He reasons from what the report describes: they live in villages, they till ground and keep herds, they cover themselves, they observe a law and a modesty. Whatever does those things reasons, and whatever reasons descends from the first man and can be preached to. Christopher, the dog-headed saint whose image the churches already keep, is the same argument carried in a picture. Behind both stands Augustine, who ruled at Hippo four centuries earlier that no strangeness of body puts a son of Adam outside the human family.
suggested_refs: Ratramnus, Epistola de Cynocephalis, Patrologia Latina 121:1153-56, not retrieved and never translated into English
Augustine, De civitate Dei XVI, on the monstrous races
sources: san_cristobal.journey.json, the Corbie and Hippo Regius stops

segments.name: The Death of Ansgar and the Succession

stops.name: Bremen, the last illness
stops.date_confidence: attested that the final illness preceded the death of 3 February 865; the exact day the words were spoken is not given
stops.campa: The archbishop falls ill and does not recover. He has wanted martyrdom his whole life, was promised it in a vision as a young man, and is now dying in bed in his own city of a sickness that will take weeks. A trusty disciple sits with him, and Robinson's edition holds that the disciple is Rimbert. The line the sick man keeps saying is not his own, it is Job answering out of the ash heap. In the same chapter a voice in a vision tells him to doubt nothing, that his sins are forgiven and that the promise made to him will be kept.
stops.quote: If we have received good at the Lord's hand, why should we not endure evil?
stops.quote_source: Ansgar in his last illness, quoting Job 2:10; Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. XL, tr. Charles H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (1921), p. 122
suggested_refs: Vita Anskarii ch. XL, the deathbed chapter, and Robinson's identification of the trusty disciple
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. XL, tr. Robinson (1921), pp. 122-123

stops.name: Bremen, the death of Ansgar
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the third of February Ansgar dies at Bremen with Rimbert beside him, thirty-four years after Louis the Pious first sent him north. His grief at the end, as his student sets it down, is not for the life but for the manner of its ending: he had not been found worthy to suffer for Christ, and the vision that promised him martyrdom had come to nothing anyone could point at. Rimbert records the verse from the psalm his master kept repeating. Robinson's English of 1921 prints it with a slip the printer never caught, and both surviving digitizations carry the slip.
stops.quote: Thou are just, O Lord, and thy judgment is righteous.
stops.quote_source: Ansgar in his last illness, quoting Psalm 119:137; Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. XL, tr. Charles H. Robinson (1921), p. 122. Thou are is the printed 1921 reading, retained here; the archive.org scan and the Fordham transcription agree against Thou art.
suggested_refs: The grave of Ansgar at Bremen, tended and later carried out of the city by Rimbert during the Viking raids
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. XL, tr. Robinson (1921), p. 122

stops.name: Bremen, elected without a dissenting voice
stops.date_confidence: attested for the unanimous election; the exact day is not recorded, only that it followed hard on the funeral
stops.campa: The funeral rites are barely finished when the clergy and people of the see name Rimbert archbishop, with no candidate from outside and no recorded dissent. No source gives the day, only that it followed hard on the burial. Adam of Bremen holds that Ansgar had designated him before dying and that at this moment he was still only in deacon's orders. That will not stand by itself: an archbishop must be a bishop, and a bishop is made by other bishops. The rest of the year goes on the road, collecting confirmations.
stops.quote: As soon as the funeral rites were accomplished, Rimbert, the author of the Life of Anskar, who was then in deacon's orders, and who had been named apparently by Anskar prior to his death as his successor, was nominated as archbishop. This nomination was subsequently accepted by Pope Nicholas.
stops.quote_source: Editorial footnote by the translator Charles H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (1921), p. 126, citing Adam of Bremen, Hist. xxvii. This is Robinson's synthesis, not primary text.
suggested_refs: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis Ecclesiae Pontificum, Book I, on the succession of 865
sources: Robinson, editorial note, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (1921), p. 126

stops.name: Frankfurt, before Louis the German
stops.date_confidence: the journey to Louis the German's court is attested; no source names where the king was holding court that year, and Frankfurt is placed here as his habitual seat, a placement and not an attestation
stops.campa: The see of Hamburg-Bremen exists because kings made it, and it is renewed by kings. Rimbert leaves the mouth of the Weser and goes up into East Francia to stand in front of Louis the German and ask confirmation of his succession to a united see that canon law does not comfortably allow. He gets it. The sources say only that he went to the king. They do not say which of his palaces the king was holding that season, and not one of them names a month.
suggested_refs: The royal confirmation of the union of Hamburg and Bremen, granted by Louis the German in 865

stops.name: Mainz, consecrated by Liudbert
stops.date_confidence: attested that Liudbert of Mainz consecrated him; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: Liudbert, archbishop of Mainz and metropolitan of the East Frankish church, lays hands on him in the cathedral above the Rhine. The consecration makes him what the election had only called him. Mainz is a long way from the marsh parishes and further still from Birka, and the men in that church are administering a province, not a mission. He will spend twenty-three years explaining to their successors why the two northern sees have to stay one. The month is not recorded, only the act and the name of the man who performed it.
suggested_refs: Mainz Cathedral, seat of the metropolitan who consecrated Rimbert in 865

stops.name: Rome, the pallium of Nicholas I
stops.date_confidence: attested that Nicholas I confirmed him with the pallium; whether Rimbert crossed the Alps in person or received it from envoys, no consulted source says, and the month is a placement
stops.campa: Nicholas I confirms him with the pallium, the strip of white wool that makes an archbishop an archbishop in Rome's reckoning, and with it the union of Hamburg and Bremen against the standing objection from Cologne, which has never accepted losing Bremen. The union will need defending again more than once in his lifetime, and every defence runs back through this cloth. Did he cross the Alps to take it from the pope's hands, or did it travel north with envoys while he stayed on the Weser? The record does not say.
suggested_refs: The papal confirmations of the Hamburg-Bremen union, contested from Cologne through the ninth century
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis, Book I, not read directly

stops.name: Hamburg, a title anchored to a ruin
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hamburg was sacked in 845 and that the see kept its name while governing from Bremen; no source places Rimbert on the Domplatz on any given day
stops.campa: The archdiocese is named for Hamburg and run from Bremen, because the Danish fleet burned Hamburg twenty years before Rimbert inherited it and the cathedral was never rebuilt on the old scale. He signs himself archbishop of a cleared site on the Elbe. The title carries anyway: Hamburg is the metropolitan claim over the whole north, over Denmark and Sweden and whatever lies past them. To give it up would be to concede that the mission has a boundary. Nobody in his lifetime proposes giving it up.
suggested_refs: The Hamburg Domplatz, site of the cathedral burned by the Danish fleet in 845
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis, Book I, not read directly

stops.name: Worms, the synod
stops.date_confidence: attested by German Wikipedia that he attended the Synod of Worms in 868; the month is a placement and nothing in the conciliar record is attributed to him personally
stops.campa: He goes south to Worms for a Frankish council on church law and discipline, one of the periodic assemblies where the empire's bishops legislate for a church whose outer edge none of them will ever see. Rimbert sits in it as the man who is the edge. The northern mission stays inside the Frankish church for exactly as long as its bishop keeps turning up at these meetings. No canon of the synod is attached to his name, no speech, no intervention. He is present. That is the record.
suggested_refs: The Synod of Worms, 868, and its canons on church law and discipline

stops.name: Bremen, Ansgar's poorhouse kept open
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact of his episcopate, undated within 865-888; no consulted source attaches a year, and the 868 in circulation is unsupported
stops.campa: Ansgar had founded a house at Bremen for the poor, one of those small institutions a bishop leaves behind that outlast his sermons. Rimbert keeps it running, and Bremen remembers him for it long after it has stopped reading what he wrote. There is no year for this, only the fact of it spread across twenty-three of them, and it belongs with the rest of the evidence about where the money of this see went: on the poor, on the sick, and on buying people back out of ships.
suggested_refs: The Bremen poorhouse founded by Ansgar and maintained by Rimbert, ancestor of the city's later charitable foundations

stops.name: Bücken on the Weser, a monastery founded
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia that he founded a monastery at Buecken; no source gives a year, the 870 in circulation is fabricated, and German Wikipedia does not mention the foundation at all
stops.campa: He founds a monastery at Bücken, upriver on the Weser, extending the network through which a Saxon diocese actually functions: land, a church, a few monks, a school, a roof for a travelling bishop. Bücken sits well upstream of the river mouth, which is where the raiding comes from, so a house there is also somewhere to put what must not be at Bremen when a fleet is sighted. This is the ordinary condition of the evidence for twenty-three years of ordinary work: one national account of him records the foundation in a single line, the other does not mention it, and neither gives a year.
suggested_refs: The collegiate church at Bücken on the Weser, whose foundation is credited to Rimbert

stops.name: Bremen, the vessels and the horse
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Robinson's introduction summarizes the Latin Vita Rimberti, which has never been translated into English and was not read directly for this file, and gives no date
stops.campa: The archbishop of a poor see with a rich raiding problem spends what he has on ransom. Viking raiding turns Christians into merchandise, and the merchandise is sold in markets his own priests can walk to. Rimbert breaks up the gold and silver vessels of his church to buy people back, and when that is gone he gives up the horse he rides. Robinson's introduction, summarizing a life of him that has never been put into English, reports it in one sentence and moves on.
stops.quote: In order to ransom Christians who had been captured by the Northmen he parted even with the gold and silver vessels of his church and with the horse which he kept for his own use.
stops.quote_source: Charles H. Robinson, Introduction to Anskar, the Apostle of the North (1921), p. 21, summarizing the anonymous Vita Rimberti, which the volume does not translate
suggested_refs: The anonymous Vita Rimberti, MGH SS rer. Germ., untranslated, the source of the ransom tradition
sources: Robinson, Introduction to Anskar, the Apostle of the North (1921), p. 21
German Wikipedia, 'Rimbert', on the Rembertistift and his reputation for care of the poor

stops.name: Hedeby, preaching at the emporium
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia that he continued to preach to the Danes at Hedeby, undated; contested emphasis, since German Wikipedia does not mention Haithabu at all and reads his episcopate as administrative and defensive instead
stops.campa: Hedeby is the largest market on the Danish frontier, a town of ramparts and jetties where amber, iron, silver and people change hands, and where the mission has kept a foothold since Ansgar's day. Rimbert goes there himself to preach rather than governing the Danish church at a distance from the Weser. That is one account of him. The German account never mentions the place and gives a man turned toward administration and the defence of his own coast. Two encyclopedias, two archbishops. Each is written as though the other did not exist.
suggested_refs: The Haithabu excavations, ramparts, harbour and market of the Danish frontier emporium

stops.name: Hedeby, the woman who sings the psalms
stops.date_confidence: tradition from the Vita Rimberti, undated; the chapter number 16 circulates with the story but could not be verified, since the Latin was not consulted
stops.campa: The hagiography written after Rimbert's death tells this as proof of his charity toward captives, and it is the one scene from his own life the tradition bothered to keep. No year is attached to it, and the chapter number that circulates with it could not be checked. In the slave market a captive woman is singing, and a man walking past the pens hears the words and knows them. She is singing the psalms, in a tongue nobody bought her speaking. She is recognized, ransomed, and set free.
suggested_refs: The Vita Rimberti's captive episodes, the fullest surviving picture of his charity
sources: Vita Rimberti, via Robinson's introduction (1921) and the Oekumenisches Heiligenlexikon; the Latin text was not read

stops.name: Schleswig, the parish on the Schlei
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the foundation under Ansgar is attested at Vita Anskarii ch. XXXIII, but nothing records the parish's ordinary years under Rimbert
stops.campa: Across the water from Hedeby, on the Schlei, the church founded in Ansgar's time keeps its priest, supplied and paid out of Bremen at real cost across a border that is not always open. An earlier chapter of the same book remembers a school on this frontier, set up so that the mission would one day have priests who already spoke the language. The Vita Anskarii records the founding; nothing records the decades afterward. A parish here is held the way a garrison is held, and for twenty-three years this one stands across the water with a priest in it and nobody writing anything down.
suggested_refs: Vita Anskarii ch. XXXIII, the founding of the church at Schleswig under royal license
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. XXXIII, tr. Robinson (1921)
general context of the Danish mission churches

stops.name: Ribe, the church King Horik II allowed
stops.date_confidence: attested that the church was founded under Ansgar by license of Horik II and that Rimbert recorded it; his own oversight of it as archbishop is inference from the office
stops.campa: At Ribe on the west coast of Jutland stands a wooden church raised by license of Horik II, one of the two footholds Ansgar won inside Denmark proper. Rimbert wrote the founding into the Vita himself, in the chapter after the one about Schleswig, and inherits the work of keeping it staffed. The building is timber. The sea road from Bremen is open about half the year. Danish tolerance for these buildings is the policy of particular kings and not a settlement between churches and crowns, so the license holding the roof up is one man's word, and the man is Horik II.
suggested_refs: Vita Anskarii ch. XXXIV, the church at Ribe granted under Horik II
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. XXXIV, tr. Robinson (1921)

stops.name: Aarhus, a church nobody can date
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; a ninth-century Christian church at Aarhus is generally accepted, but whether its founding belongs to Ansgar's lifetime or Rimbert's own episcopate is contested among historians and is not resolved here
stops.campa: A Christian church stands at Aarhus in the ninth century and the sources cannot agree whose it is. Some place the founding in Ansgar's lifetime, some inside Rimbert's own episcopate, and the question has stayed open. Either way it falls inside the field he answers for: one more wooden building on a Danish shore, one more priest to supply from the Weser, one more congregation that can be gone in a season if the local lord changes his mind about what he tolerates. Whether he built it or only inherited it is still argued.
suggested_refs: The disputed ninth-century church at Aarhus, claimed for both Ansgar and Rimbert
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, on the Danish churches
founding date and founder contested among historians; no consulted source settles it

stops.name: The Danish royal court, a tolerance renewed each year
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the general pattern of Ansgar-era and Rimbert-era mission diplomacy; the court was itinerant and no source fixes a meeting place or a date
stops.campa: The whole Danish mission rests on an arrangement and not on a conversion. The kings tolerate preaching inside their territory; no king accepts baptism. Rimbert keeps the arrangement Ansgar struck, going to the court wherever the court is, bringing gifts, asking for licenses, and never once getting the thing that would make the licenses unnecessary. No source names a meeting place, a date, or what was carried there. The court moves through its own country and the mission follows it. The arrangement holds twenty-three years.
suggested_refs: The itinerant Danish royal court of the later ninth century, on whose tolerance the mission churches depended
sources: general pattern of the Danish mission, no single document

stops.name: Birka, the Swedish mission held at arm's length
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Birka mission continued under Rimbert's oversight; whether he ever crossed to Björkö himself is not stated in any consulted source
stops.campa: Birka on its island in Lake Mälaren is the furthest thing the see claims, reached by Ansgar twice by sea and held afterward by letters and by whatever priest can be persuaded to sail. Whether Rimbert ever made the crossing himself the record does not say, and the silence is not the kind that can be argued away. What he does say, writing about his master's voyage, is what such a crossing costs, and he says it in the first person, as a man who has the route by report from the one companion who came back.
stops.quote: How great and serious were the calamities which he suffered while engaged in this mission, father Witmar, who himself shared them, can best tell. It may suffice for me to say that while they were in the midst of their journey they fell into the hands of pirates.
stops.quote_source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. X, tr. Charles H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (1921), p. 47
suggested_refs: The Birka excavations on Björkö, including the crosses and crucifixes found in women's graves
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. X, tr. Robinson (1921), p. 47
Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, introduction to the Vita Anskarii

stops.name: Bremen, the life of his master begun
stops.date_confidence: attested that Rimbert wrote the Vita Anskarii and dedicated it to the monks of Corbie; composition is dated 869-876 by English Wikipedia and c. 876 by German Wikipedia, and the year here is a placement inside that window
stops.campa: He writes the life of his master out of memory and out of papers he has kept, and he addresses it to the monks of Corbie in Picardy, the house that trained Ansgar and sent him north. The dedication does not come from Rimbert alone. It comes from the sons and disciples together, a whole household writing back to the mother house to report what became of the man they lent it. Ratramnus is in that same cloister. The book goes south along the road his answer about the dog-headed men had come north on.
stops.quote: The sons and disciples of the most reverend Father Anskar, to whom has been granted everlasting happiness, salute the holy fathers and brethren who are God's soldiers in the sacred monastery of Corbey, to whom special veneration and affection in the love of Christ are due, and they pray for the peace and safety of those who rule over them in the Lord.
stops.quote_source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. I, opening dedication, tr. Charles H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (1921), p. 25
suggested_refs: Corbie Abbey in Picardy, mother house of the Saxon mission and addressee of the Vita Anskarii
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, ch. I, tr. Robinson (1921), p. 25

stops.name: Bremen, what the book is for
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia as the aims of the work; the year is a placement inside the composition window
stops.campa: The Vita Anskarii is a saint's life and it is also a working document with three jobs. It argues that the union of Hamburg and Bremen is legitimate, against Cologne and against anyone in Rome inclined to reopen the question. It sets the northern mission in front of Frankish clergy in terms that might make a man volunteer for it. It reminds West Frankish patrons that the endowment taken back at Turholt was taken from something real. Rimbert writes as a witness rather than a compiler, and says so in his own prologue.
suggested_refs: The prologue of the Vita Anskarii, in which Rimbert states his standing as an eyewitness
sources: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii, prologue, tr. Robinson (1921)

stops.name: Bremen, the book and its long disappearance
stops.date_confidence: contradiction carried: English Wikipedia dates the work between 869 and 876, German Wikipedia gives c. 876. The 873 in circulation is a midpoint no source states and is not used.
stops.campa: The book is finished somewhere inside a window nobody can close. One authority gives 869 to 876; another gives 876 flat; no source gives a year in between that would settle it. Its afterlife is rougher than its dating. The oldest copy to survive was made a full century after Rimbert died, the Codex Stuttgardiensis. The text drops out of use after Adam of Bremen reads it in the eleventh century, and is not printed again until Philip Caesar brings it out in 1642, close to six hundred years later.
suggested_refs: Codex Stuttgardiensis G.32, tenth century, the oldest surviving manuscript of the Vita Anskarii
Philip Caesar, Triapostolatus septentrionis (1642), which returned the lost text to circulation
sources: Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, introduction to the Vita Anskarii

stops.name: Bremen, out of the city with Ansgar's bones
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the episode comes from Adam of Bremen writing two centuries later and was not checked against the Gesta directly, and no year is given
stops.campa: Viking pressure on the Weser and the Elbe gets bad enough that the cathedral clergy leave the city. What happened next is reported by Adam of Bremen, writing two hundred years afterward with his own reasons for wanting the succession to look like devotion, and he gives no year for it. Rimbert goes out of Bremen carrying Ansgar's relics and the church treasure with him: the second archbishop of the north on the road away from a fleet, with the first archbishop of the north in his arms.
suggested_refs: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis, Book I, on the Viking raids of Rimbert's later episcopate
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis, Book I, not read directly for this file

stops.name: Stade, watching the water
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the general pattern of Elbe-basin administration; no document places Rimbert at Stade on any date
stops.campa: Stade sits on the lower Elbe where the river widens toward the sea, a secondary centre of the diocese and a place from which a man can watch what is coming up the water. In these years the see is administered from wherever it is safe to administer it, and the safe places change with the season and the tide. The town's role leaves no scene behind it, only an arrangement that must have existed, because the diocese went on working through years when Bremen itself was not safe. No charter puts Rimbert at Stade on any day of his life.
suggested_refs: Stade on the lower Elbe, secondary administrative centre of the Hamburg-Bremen archdiocese
sources: general context of Hamburg-Bremen's Elbe-basin administration; no specific document

stops.name: Ramelsloh, the refuge founded by the other man
stops.date_confidence: the chapter at Ramelsloh is attested from 845, founded by Ansgar in flight from the burning of Hamburg; the story that Rimbert retreated here in the 880s is not supported by the German record and appears to be Ansgar's flight doubled back onto his successor
stops.campa: Ramelsloh, inland from the Elbe, holds a college of canons founded in 845, when Ansgar reached the place fleeing the Vikings and needed somewhere to put his clergy. It is Rimbert's to govern, one more house in a network built out of flight. The chronicle tradition that has Rimbert himself retreating here forty years later looks like the same story told twice with a different man in it. The refuge is real. The second flight to it is not documented anywhere that can be checked.
suggested_refs: The collegiate chapter at Ramelsloh, first mentioned 845, later drawn on for Archbishop Unwan's Hamburg chapter
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis, Book I, not read directly

stops.name: Hilgenrieder Bucht, the archbishop in the field at Norditi
stops.date_confidence: attested by both English and German Wikipedia for the year 884 and the outcome; the month is unrecorded, and the pin follows German Wikipedia's placement of the engagement in the former Hilgenrieder Bucht rather than the inland coordinates in circulation
stops.campa: On the East Frisian coast, in a shallow bay that has since silted up into farmland, a Viking army is met and broken by a Frisian force the archbishop of Bremen has raised and is commanding in person. The victory is complete enough that no Viking army occupies East Frisia again. He is a bishop of about fifty-four, in a war fought by farmers on their own ground, and he has spent twenty years buying captives back from the men he is now meeting in the field. The year given is 884. The bay is dry land now, in the municipality of Hagermarsch.
suggested_refs: The site of the Battle of Norditi in the former Hilgenrieder Bucht, municipality of Hagermarsch
sources: German Wikipedia on the 884 engagement and its location

segments.name: The Last Grants and the Grave

stops.name: Bremen, the market, the mint, and the toll
stops.date_confidence: attested for 888; the grantor's title is corrected here, since Arnulf of Carinthia was King of East Francia from November 887 and was not crowned emperor until February 896, eight years after both the grant and Rimbert's death
stops.campa: In the last year of his life Rimbert obtains from Arnulf, newly elected king of the East Franks, the grant of market, coinage and toll rights to Bremen. The city may hold a market, strike silver and take tolls, and the man who holds the rights is the archbishop. It is the foundation of Bremen's later wealth and of the archbishopric's standing as a temporal power on the Weser. Nearly every account of the grant calls Arnulf emperor. He was crowned emperor in 896, eight years after this charter and eight years after Rimbert was in the ground.
suggested_refs: The 888 diploma of King Arnulf granting market, coinage and toll rights to Bremen

stops.name: Bremen, the eleventh of June
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Rimbert dies at Bremen on the eleventh of June, twenty-three years after burying Ansgar in the same city. He had come to the see as the last man alive who had heard the northern mission described by the person who invented it. He leaves it with the Danish churches still standing, the Swedish mission still nominal, the poorhouse still open, and the union of the two sees intact. The book he wrote will outlive all of it and go unread for six hundred years in the middle. He is fifty-eight, or near it; nobody wrote down the year he was born.
suggested_refs: The Vita Rimberti, written within a generation at Corvey, which closes his life as he had closed his master's
sources: Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, introduction to the Vita Anskarii

stops.name: Bremen, the outer wall beside Willehad
stops.date_confidence: the burial tradition is recorded by the Oekumenisches Heiligenlexikon, which places him at the outer wall of Bremen cathedral next to Willehad; no tomb monument, inscription or archaeologically confirmed grave is documented, and the day of burial is a placement
stops.campa: He is put in the ground at the outer wall of Bremen cathedral, next to Willehad, the first bishop of Bremen, a hundred years dead. The tradition names the spot and nothing else confirms it: no monument, no inscription, no excavation. The cathedral's own list of archbishop burials does not carry him. Two men lie along that wall in the story, the first bishop of the place and the man who wrote the life of the first archbishop of the north. Nothing has been dug up along it to confirm either grave.
suggested_refs: The exterior wall of Bremen Cathedral and the grave of Willehad, first bishop of Bremen
sources: Bremer Dom history pages, checked and silent on his grave

stops.name: Bremen, Adalgar takes the see
stops.date_confidence: attested that Adalgar, his assistant, succeeded him in 888; the month is a placement
stops.campa: Adalgar, his assistant, takes the see. The union holds and the office continues, but the northern journeys stop. No archbishop of this line is recorded dying on mission again until Unni is buried at Birka in 936, forty-eight years later. Both men who knew the north from inside it are now in the ground at Bremen, and the second of them had written the only account either of them left. Did the mission stop in those forty-eight years, or only the writing about it?
suggested_refs: Fordham's introduction to the Vita Anskarii, noting Unni's death at Birka in 936 as the next mission death of the line
sources: Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, introduction to the Vita Anskarii

stops.name: Bremen, two feast days and a foundation
stops.date_confidence: the St.-Remberti-Stift is dated c. 1300; the feast dates are liturgical usage carried forward, and the year here marks the foundation rather than the beginning of the cult, which is medieval and undated
stops.campa: Bremen keeps him. He is venerated as a saint from the Middle Ages on, honored for care of the poor and the sick rather than for the battle or the book. His feast is kept on the eleventh of June, the day he died, and also on the fourth of February in the dioceses of Hamburg and Osnabrück, where the memorial is optional. Both dates are real and the calendars have never agreed. Around 1300 a charitable foundation in the city takes his name, and it is open under it still, the Rembertistift.
suggested_refs: The St.-Remberti-Stift in Bremen, charitable foundation of c. 1300 carrying his name into the present
sources: Oekumenisches Heiligenlexikon, 'Rimbert', on the 11 June and 4 February observances
